title: Binary trees: a second look
body:
Draw the tree. Follow a pointer.
Pause a call. Return to its caller.

Y13 • Cambridge 9618
VB.NET • 2D arrays and records
notes: Plan 70–80 minutes or split into two lessons. Core goal: a safe in-order traversal, explained through calls and returns. No OOP knowledge needed. Omit extensions if pupils need more tracing time.

title: What we are practising
body:
1. Draw and label a tree.
2. Convert links into row indexes.
3. Trace a small recursive traversal.
4. Complete and test InOrder.
notes: Success means explaining where a paused call resumes, not merely reciting sorted output. Use Tasks 1–2 for 15–20 min, Task 3 for 20 min, Task 4 for 10 min, Task 5A for 5 min, Task 6 for 15–20 min.

title: A tree we can draw
body:
Insert 8, 3, 12, 6 in that order.
Start at the root for each new value.
Smaller goes left; larger goes right.

Where does 6 go? Why?
notes: Reveal or draw incrementally on the board. 6 < 8, then 6 > 3. Thus right child of 3, inside the left subtree of 8. Values are distinct; no duplicate rule is needed.
footer: Task 1 • Draw a fresh sketch after each insertion

title: The whole subtree matters
body:
Each node has at most two children.
A leaf has no children.
A subtree includes its root and everything below it.

The BST rule applies to the entire subtree.
notes: Root: 8. Leaves: 6 and 12. Left subtree of 8: 3 and 6. A binary tree need not be ordered. Check Task 1 before moving on.

title: A pointer stores an index
body:
Columns: 0 = left, 1 = data, 2 = right.
-1 means there is no child.
RootPointer is the index of the root.
notes: Keep the earlier lesson column convention. A cell containing 3 in a pointer column means row 3; data 3 is a different concept. Task 2 uses different data.

title: Following a pointer in two steps
body:
TreeArray(1, 2) = 3
Read the right pointer in row 1.

TreeArray(3, 1) = 6
Read the data in row 3.
notes: Ask students to point physically to the pointer cell, row label, then data cell. Never pass data as though it were a row index.
footer: Task 2 • Complete the table, then reconstruct a different tree

title: One job for each call
body:
InOrder(p) means:
output the subtree whose root is at index p.

Each call remembers its own p
and where to continue after its child returns.
notes: Use three paper frames labelled p=0, p=1, p=2 plus -1 frames. Do not introduce code yet. The index labels must stay visible.

title: The empty subtree
body:
When p = -1, return immediately.
Read no array cell. Output nothing.

A leaf still has two empty subtrees.
code:
If p = -1 Then
    Exit Sub
End If
notes: This is a deliberate change from the previous lesson, which checked child pointers before calling. Here the procedure accepts -1, so the starting tree can also be empty. Both are valid designs; use only this one today.

title: The in-order recipe
body:
For the subtree at p:

1. If p = -1, return.
2. Do the whole left subtree.
3. Output this node’s data.
4. Do the whole right subtree.
5. Return to the caller.
notes: Left, node, right applies at every node, not just the original root. Put your finger on the current rule. The caller pauses while a child call runs.

title: A leaf takes three calls
body:
Start InOrder(1), where data = 3.
Its two child pointers are -1.
notes: There are three invocations counting the leaf and its two empty calls. Returning from an empty child resumes the leaf, rather than finishing the whole traversal.

title: The root waits
body:
Start InOrder(0).
It calls InOrder(1).
The root call waits before its output.

After the left call finishes,
p=0 resumes and outputs 8.
notes: Physical rehearsal: teacher holds the root frame; a pupil performs the left leaf and hands control back. Ask: what is p in the resumed call? Answer 0. It was not permanently replaced by 1.

title: A complete three-node trace
body: All arguments below are indexes.
notes: Expand each empty call and return orally. Task 3 deliberately uses a non-BST so sorting cannot substitute for a trace.
footer: Task 3 • Draw first, then act out all calls and returns

title: A checkpoint before coding
body:
When the left subtree finishes:

Which call resumes?
What is its p?
Which instruction comes next?

Use your paper frames to explain.
notes: For the worked tree: root call InOrder(0), p=0, output TreeArray(0,1)=8. If pupils cannot answer, repeat the leaf and root activities before Task 4. Do not advance merely because final output is correct.

title: Your turn to complete the code
body:
Use the recipe to fill Task 4.

Check for -1 before any array access.
Pass a child’s index to each call.
Output the data between those calls.
notes: Keep the full solution on the following slide hidden until pupils have attempted Task 4. Support: ask what each column means; do not simply dictate the numbers.
footer: Task 4 • Explain each gap as well as filling it

title: The complete in-order procedure
body:
Each call gets its own local p.
The caller resumes after a child call.

Start with InOrder(RootPointer).
code:
Sub InOrder(ByVal p As Integer)
    If p = -1 Then
        Exit Sub
    End If
    InOrder(TreeArray(p, 0))
    Console.WriteLine(TreeArray(p, 1))
    InOrder(TreeArray(p, 2))
End Sub
notes: Reveal after Task 4. Gap answers: -1, Exit Sub, 0, 1, 2. With RootPointer=-1 there is no output and no array access. ByVal helps pupils see that each invocation has its own parameter value.

title: Two checks for broken code
body:
Safety: does the -1 check happen first?
Order: is the output between the calls?
code:
' Check the order of these actions
Check for -1
Call left subtree
Output current data
Call right subtree
notes: Task 5A: accessing row -1 before the guard crashes. Moving the guard first prevents that, but output first is pre-order, so the output also needs to move between the child calls.
footer: Task 5A • Explain both bugs before repairing them

title: Testing one idea at a time
body:
Predict first, then run each test.
Use the supplied table; no insertion code needed.
table: The parameter sets the starting root
notes: Task 6. Starter contains a deliberate TODO. Main test tree is 40,20,60,30. Expected in-order 20,30,40,60; subtree 1 gives 20,30; leaf 2 gives 60; -1 gives no output.

title: Optional: a different output position
body:
In-order: left, OUTPUT, right.
Post-order: left, right, OUTPUT.

The same guard and child pointers work.
Try Task 5B after your in-order trace is secure.
notes: Worked tree post-order: 3,12,8. Task 1 tree: 30,20,60,40. Optional extension only. Recursive search and recursive insertion are deferred.

title: Optional: records store the same fields
body:
A record groups the three integers.
Its child pointers still store indexes.
All child pointers must be initialised to -1.
code:
Structure NodeRecord
    Public LeftPointer As Integer
    Public Data As Integer
    Public RightPointer As Integer
End Structure
Dim Nodes(3) As NodeRecord

' Array:  TreeArray(p, 0)
' Record: Nodes(p).LeftPointer
notes: This is a record with fields only, no methods or constructors. VB.NET default integers are 0, so explicitly set both child pointers to -1. Optional booklet extension contains the translation task. No chapter 20 concepts are required.

title: Exit check
body:
Root: data 8 at index 2.
Only child: data 5 at index 0, on the left.

Draw it. Give the first call and output.
Where does the root call resume
after its left call?
notes: Answer: InOrder(2). Output 5,8. Root call resumes at Console.WriteLine(TreeArray(p,1)) with p=2. If pupils say p=0 or that the whole traversal ends at the leaf, reteach calls and returns.
footer: Next practice • Repeat on a new shape before adding search
